Renderers evaluate light transport by tracing how emission and reflection contribute along paths to an image.
Rendering equation and numerical integration
At surface point , outgoing radiance in direction consists of emitted light and reflected incoming light:

is emitted radiance, incoming radiance, the BRDF, the normal, and the hemisphere above the surface. The cosine accounts for projected area. Visibility determines whether geometry blocks a sampled direction. Incoming radiance depends on radiance leaving other surfaces, so the equation is recursive. Expanding it produces paths of light bounces: direct light reaches a surface then camera; indirect light includes more interactions. The transport equation remains the same for every material; material response changes through the BRDF. Fresnel reflection makes many dielectrics more reflective at grazing angles. CMU-16

An integral accumulates a continuous range of contributions. Midpoint quadrature evaluates the center of each interval; trapezoidal quadrature joins endpoint samples; Simpson’s rule fits a quadratic. These deterministic rules work well for smooth low-dimensional functions. Visibility boundaries create discontinuities, and multidimensional light paths become expensive for tensor grids: samples per dimension require evaluations in dimension . CMU-17
Monte Carlo integration uses random samples. If is drawn from density , then

The weighting follows from expectation: . Density must be positive wherever contributes and measured in the same domain as the integral. The estimator is unbiased, but random error remains. For independent samples , variance of the mean is , so standard deviation decreases as . Four times as many samples roughly halves noise. CMU-17 · CMU-18

For a small numerical trace, integrate over the unit interval; the exact answer is . Uniform samples produce mean square . The discrepancy is sampling error. A proposal density that resembles the integrand makes weighted samples less variable. For , the exact integral is 1. Uniform sampling has contribution and variance . Sampling instead from makes for almost every sample, yielding zero variance. Real rendering integrals are more complex, but the example explains importance sampling. CMU-18 · CMU-19
From the rendering equation to paths

Use operator notation , where represents one reflection-and-visibility step. Substitution yields . The term is direct emission at the point. includes paths that reflect once before reaching emission. includes two reflections, and so on. Path tracing estimates this infinite series by following random directions and accumulating weighted contributions. Absorption and energy loss usually make long-path contributions diminish, but some environments preserve light for many bounces.

Direct-light sampling selects a source and tests visibility to it. If the source is small, sampling a random hemisphere direction may almost never hit it. Conversely, sampling only the light may miss glossy paths where material response concentrates energy. The path formulation clarifies that the challenge is to place probability mass on path configurations that carry large contribution. CMU-16 · CMU-18 · CMU-19
One-bounce Monte Carlo estimator
For a surface point, estimate reflected radiance by sampling directions from density and evaluating the BRDF, incoming radiance, and cosine. For samples, the estimate is

Each symbol has a specific role: emits from the surface; redirects incoming light; is the radiance arriving from the sampled direction; is the surface normal; is the directional sampling density; and the cosine is projected area. Visibility is included in by making it zero when geometry blocks that direction. If the PDF is expressed per unit area rather than per unit solid angle, it must first be converted. CMU-16 · CMU-18

The estimator is an expectation written as a sample average. If directions are drawn uniformly over a hemisphere, the probability density per unit solid angle is , because the hemisphere has solid angle . Substituting that density into the one-sample contribution multiplies the integrand by . The cosine still matters: a ray arriving nearly tangent to a surface contributes little projected flux, while a ray arriving near the normal contributes more. This gives a useful importance distribution. Since , the density is normalized. Sampling with this density cancels the cosine in the estimator, leaving for each sampled direction. The code becomes simpler and, when incident radiance is roughly constant, the samples are allocated in proportion to the part of the integrand that matters. CMU-18

Another proposal samples a finite area light directly. Let be the shaded point and a point on the emitter. Write for their distance, and let be the angle between the emitter’s normal and the direction from toward . A patch of emitter area subtends solid angle

This is a change of variables: the same visible set of light samples is being described on the emitter surface instead of as directions at . Therefore the integrand must acquire the Jacobian . The surface’s own projected-area cosine at remains as well, along with visibility, which is zero when an occluder blocks the segment. With uniform area samples, the estimator multiplies the average by the emitter area. This avoids wasting most rays on empty sky when the emitter subtends only a small part of the hemisphere. In the lecture’s square-light / blocker / ground-plane comparison, 100 uniform hemisphere samples are grainy, while 100 area-light samples produce a much smoother shadow and illumination field; the area-light result remains strong at 16 samples, and even its one-sample result compares favorably to uniform sampling. The lesson is about variance per unit computation, not a guarantee that every single random estimate will look clean. CMU-18

The path version multiplies a throughput term by the sampled BRDF, cosine, and inverse density at each bounce. A path contribution might be written . Here is bounce count, and each factor belongs to one interaction. Long paths can have very small throughput; Russian roulette terminates them stochastically and compensates survivors by dividing by continuation probability. This is an estimator design choice, not a physical event that must occur in the scene. CMU-18 · CMU-19

Why does path tracing recurse? At one surface, the rendering equation asks for incoming radiance from every direction. A ray in one sampled direction either reaches an emitter or hits another surface; in the second case, the next surface has the same integral to evaluate. Thus one random path is a chain of surface interactions from the camera toward an emitter. Even a single path estimate has the correct expected value when every sampled direction is weighted by its probability density, but individual paths are noisy; averaging many independent paths reduces variance. Limiting paths to direct illumination gives hard, dark regions wherever a surface receives no direct source. Adding indirect bounces fills some of those regions. Longer paths matter selectively: a glass lantern may look black if paths stop before the sequence of reflection and refraction events that transports light through it, while four-bounce paths can reveal its glass structure. CMU-18

Russian roulette makes path termination probabilistic. Suppose a candidate path has contribution and the renderer keeps it with probability . On a surviving path, use ; on a terminated path, use zero. The expected result is

The estimate therefore remains unbiased even though some paths are skipped. A deterministic rule such as “discard every contribution below a threshold” would systematically remove dim light and bias the answer. In the lecture’s example, more aggressive termination shortens rendering time while making shadows noisier; the useful setting depends on how much remaining throughput the scene carries and how much variance the renderer can tolerate. CMU-18
Bidirectional path construction

Camera-only path tracing launches a path from the camera and samples successive surface directions. This is effective when important paths are easy to find from the camera side. It struggles with difficult light connections, such as a small opening that admits illumination into a room or a caustic where light focuses through specular events. Bidirectional path tracing also launches subpaths from emitters and connects light-side and camera-side vertices. It can discover a connection even when neither a camera-only nor a light-only random walk would likely create the entire path.

The estimator must account for the probability of generating a path by every strategy that could have produced it. Multiple importance weights compare those path densities so the same contribution is not overcounted. Path length is itself a sampling decision: short paths often represent direct illumination; longer ones capture more indirect transport but may have diminishing contribution and higher cost. Russian roulette can end long low-throughput paths without a fixed bounce cutoff. CMU-19
Metropolis light transport as a path-space walk
Metropolis-Hastings sampling creates a Markov chain whose states are light paths. From current path , propose new path with transition density and accept it with probability

where is the target path-contribution distribution. The ratio corrects for asymmetric proposal probabilities. Rejected proposals keep the current path, maintaining the desired stationary distribution. In rendering, path mutations can explore regions where image contribution is large, reusing promising paths rather than restarting from scratch. This can help with rare, high-energy transport, but chains need sufficient exploration and careful normalization; correlation among samples changes variance behavior. CMU-19
Photon mapping and radiosity

Photon mapping traces particles of light from sources and stores where they hit surfaces. At a shading point, nearby photon contributions estimate incoming illumination. The estimate is a density estimate: using too large a neighborhood blurs detail, while too small a neighborhood has high variance. Photon maps can represent caustics that camera-side random paths rarely find. They are often biased at finite neighborhood radius, with bias decreasing as the estimate is refined.

Radiosity divides diffuse surfaces into patches and solves for energy exchange among them. A form factor describes what fraction of energy leaving one patch reaches another. The discrete system couples all patches; dense systems can be expensive, while spatial hierarchy or iterative methods reduce work. Radiosity assumes diffuse response and typically solves a global energy balance, whereas path tracing samples individual transport paths. These approaches target related light transport from different numerical angles. CMU-19
Recursive light paths: shadows, mirrors, glass, and sampled effects

A shadow query asks whether any blocker lies between a surface point and a light. This is a binary visibility test, so a shadow ray can stop at its first valid hit instead of finding the closest blocker. The local illumination may still contain an ambient term, but ambient light in this basic model is a constant hack that prevents completely black unlit regions; it is not a simulation of bounced light. A point light yields hard shadow boundaries. An area light is a continuum of positions, each with a different visibility result; sampling positions and averaging estimates the lit fraction. Fully blocked samples form the umbra, fully visible samples the lit region, and a mixture forms the penumbra. If a shadow ray starts exactly at the hit, floating-point error may report the surface itself as a blocker, creating self-shadow speckles. Start at or require a candidate parameter , with chosen relative to scene scale. MITG-11 (00:07:40–00:20:20)
For an ideal mirror, reflect the incoming direction across the surface normal. Given a unit normal and incident unit direction pointing toward the surface, the outgoing direction is

The formula subtracts twice the normal projection, flipping its sign while leaving the tangential component unchanged. A secondary ray from the hit point travels along ; its returned radiance contributes to the original hit color. This is recursive: the reflected ray may strike another mirror and launch another ray. Real surfaces are imperfect. Fresnel reflection describes the increase in reflectance at grazing angles, where a surface looks more mirror-like. Schlick’s inexpensive approximation is , where is the normal-incidence reflectance. It retains the angle trend with only a dot product and a fifth power. MITG-11 (00:20:20–00:30:20)

Refraction changes direction across an interface because light travels at different speeds in different materials. Snell’s law is , where are refractive indices and angles are measured relative to the normal. To compute the new vector without inverse trigonometric functions, take unit incident direction pointing toward the viewer in the lecture’s convention and a suitably oriented unit normal . Define and . The transmitted direction can be written

The tangential component is scaled according to Snell’s law; the normal component is chosen to keep and point into the second medium. The sign convention for and must be consistent—many implementations use an incident vector pointing toward the surface and flip the normal when exiting. As a worked case, for air to glass with and incidence angle , Snell gives , so : the ray bends toward the normal. From glass to air at a sufficiently grazing angle, the square-root radicand becomes negative; there is no real transmitted direction, and the event is total internal reflection. Fiber optics use repeated internal reflections to guide light. MITG-11 (00:30:20–00:54:55)

Reflection and refraction are only some of the possible branches. Rainbows require wavelength-dependent refraction plus internal reflection in water droplets; tracing only one RGB ray cannot reproduce the full dispersion without modeling several wavelengths. Caustics—bright focused patterns from curved reflective or refractive surfaces—are hard for camera-launched paths because the important light paths occupy a small set of directions. The lecture also uses ray tracing as a forward model for lens design and caustic shaping: alter a glass surface, trace rays through it, and optimize the resulting pattern. These effects distinguish recursive specular paths from general global illumination. MITG-11 (00:54:55–01:03:20)

Sampling adds realistic variation and computational cost. Perturbing a perfect mirror ray can approximate a rough or brushed surface, but a single independent random direction per pixel appears as white noise. Repeating samples and averaging reduces variance. Choosing random points on an area light estimates soft shadows; choosing positions in a lens aperture gives depth of field; sampling scene time gives motion blur; multiple samples within a pixel reduce jagged edges. If each branch creates new rays to depth , a full ray tree may contain rays, so costs grow rapidly. Renderers cap recursion depth or terminate branches whose remaining energy is negligible. This still leaves unequal work across pixels: a small background ray may hit many detailed objects while another hits a simple surface, so static allocation can leave processors idle. MITG-11 (01:03:20–01:19:04)
Global illumination solves a coupled light transport problem

Direct lighting accounts for light that reaches a surface from explicit sources. It misses the red tint that a red wall contributes to a nearby floor, soft indirect fill, and many caustics. Backward ray tracing starts at the eye because rays that reach the eye are the ones worth computing, but physical light travels from source to eye. Reversing path direction is valid for ordinary reciprocal reflection; it does not mean the algorithm has simulated every light path. MITG-16 (00:04:49–00:16:10)

Using the rendering equation defined earlier, outgoing radiance at a surface point depends on emitted radiance and the visible hemisphere of incoming reflected radiance. Its terms are the BRDF, incoming radiance, surface normal, and projected-area cosine. Because incoming radiance itself comes from other surfaces’ outgoing radiance, this integral couples positions and directions throughout the scene. A finite approximation can be solved as a large linear system (radiosity is one family), but general high-dimensional scenes make this expensive. MITG-16 (00:16:12–00:26:33)
Monte Carlo rendering estimates the integral by random samples. If directions are drawn from a probability density , an unbiased estimate is

The division by compensates for where samples are concentrated: sampling a region twice as often must not make that region count twice as much. Direct light sampling is usually added explicitly because a small, bright source is unlikely to be hit by a random hemisphere direction. MITG-16 (00:26:50–00:31:34; 01:16:00–01:19:14)

A naïve recursive integrator takes many samples at each bounce, so work grows exponentially: 100 directions at each of two bounces means roughly paths. Path tracing takes one sampled continuation at each hit, then averages many independent paths per pixel. Each path is noisy, but cost grows approximately linearly with path count rather than with a branch factor at every bounce. With independent samples, Monte Carlo standard error typically decreases as ; four times as many samples roughly halves noise. Bright, rare paths cause shot noise, which is especially visible around glossy reflections or small sources. MITG-16 (00:27:02–00:43:35)

Irradiance caching and photon mapping reuse work with different coordinates. Irradiance caching stores expensive indirect-light estimates at selected image pixels and interpolates nearby values, while checking that hit geometry and normals are similar. It adds samples around image-space edges where indirect illumination changes quickly. Its error can show the cache spacing in smooth regions. Photon mapping first emits photons forward from light sources, storing position and energy at surface hits; a camera pass then gathers nearby photon records. This puts reusable samples in scene space instead of current-view image space. Neither method is exact: each trades time for blur, density artifacts, or biased reconstruction. MITG-16 (00:43:35–01:00:00)

Subsurface scattering requires a broader material response than a BRDF. A BSSRDF relates incoming light at one surface point and direction to outgoing light at another point and direction. This models light entering skin or wax and emerging nearby, so the path can move laterally inside the material. MITG-16 (01:00:00–01:02:57)

Sampling plans matter because the integration domain is high dimensional: each bounce adds more coordinates. A regular grid can be effective in low dimensions, but grid cost scales like for samples per axis in dimension , and regular patterns can alias against scene structure. Random Monte Carlo error has a weaker dimension dependence but converges slowly. Importance sampling chooses a density proportional to expected contribution—such as the BRDF lobe—then divides by that density to remain unbiased. A bright source outside the chosen lobe can still be missed, so hybrid samplers combine BRDF sampling with direct-light samples or broader exploration. Stratification divides the domain into cells and jitters one sample per cell to avoid accidentally leaving large regions empty. MITG-16 (01:03:01–01:22:37)

The coordinate-axis rotation matrices from P3-03 are easy to construct, so transform the arbitrary axis until it coincides with the z axis, rotate by the desired angle , then undo those alignment transforms. Color and the simplified local-lighting model

A physical surface does not simply “have” a color independent of illumination. Light has a spectrum; a material absorbs and reflects portions of it; the eye integrates the resulting spectrum. The course reduces this continuous process to three RGB channels because it is practical for graphics hardware. In normalized RGB, each channel ranges from 0 to 1: red is , green , blue , white , black . Equal channel values lie along the gray diagonal. An 8-bit-per-channel buffer stores RGB combinations. RGB is additive light: red plus green light can appear yellow. Pigments and printing are better described with subtractive CMY/CMYK, so mixing crayon colors is not the same operation as adding display light. HLS/HSL and HSV-like models rearrange color coordinates into hue and intensity/saturation controls that are easier for a person to choose. HSL lightness and HSV value are not the same coordinate, despite the lecture’s shorthand. (P3-08)

The full light-transport problem contains repeated bounces: a wall illuminates a table, the table illuminates another wall, and those contributions continue. Physically based global illumination can approximate this energy exchange, but the introductory fixed-function model makes a deliberately simple local approximation. It treats background illumination as a constant ambient term, a point light as a source with a position and RGB color, and a material as a set of per-channel response coefficients. This is a teaching model, not an accurate description of metals, glass, or all real surfaces. (P3-08)

For diffuse reflection, let be a unit surface normal and a unit direction from the surface toward the light. Lambert’s cosine law gives the orientation factor . When the light grazes the surface, the cosine approaches zero; when it faces the normal, it is one. The useful rendering form clamps the back-facing case: . If and , then . A red diffuse material with coefficient under unit red light contributes red before ambient and specular terms. A unit normal matters: otherwise the dot product also scales by vector lengths and ceases to be the cosine. Polygon normals can be found from the cross product of two edges; reverse edge order reverses the normal. (P3-08)

Ambient light is a shortcut for many indirect bounces. It brightens surfaces even when the explicit point light does not reach them, but because it is constant it cannot create realistic spatially varying indirect illumination or cast shadows. The lecture’s per-channel local model can be written in an explanatory normalized form:

For a shiny highlight, classical Phong compares the view direction with the ideal reflected direction and raises their cosine to a gloss exponent. The power makes the peak narrow: for , drops far more quickly away from than . Blinn’s practical variant uses the halfway direction and the factor . The halfway vector is easy to compute and yields the Blinn–Phong model used in many introductory renderers. A larger exponent narrows the highlight and makes the object look glossier; it does not mean the material is physically more reflective at every angle. This model explains why a plastic toy can look convincing but a metal or dielectric is harder: it compresses complex microfacet behavior into a few tunable values. The instructor maps those values to creative controls. A texture changes surface color; bump mapping perturbs the normal used by the lighting calculation, changing apparent small-scale relief without changing the silhouette; moving the light changes and highlight position; changing alters gloss. The orange example makes the normal role intuitive: perturb normals over a smooth orange-colored sphere and the light response starts to resemble textured peel. (P3-08)
Shadow representations: geometry, volumes, and depth maps

A shadow is a visibility question from the light. A surface point is directly lit if the segment from that point toward a light source is unobstructed. Three representation choices in the 2009 lectures answer that question in different spaces: project a fake shadow polygon onto a floor, construct a 3D shadow volume and count crossings, or render a depth map from the light and compare depths. (P3-18, P3-19)
For a point light , object point , and receiver plane through with normal , the ray from the light through the object is . A projected shadow point lies on the plane, so

Then . If the denominator is zero, the line is parallel to the plane (or lies wholly in it), so there is no unique projected point. For a simple numeric check, let the floor be , light , and object point . Along the ray the z coordinate is . Setting it to zero gives , so the projected point is , farther from the light’s vertical axis than the object because the light ray diverges. The projected polygon can be drawn dark and offset slightly from the floor to avoid z-fighting. It is efficient and useful for contact shadows, but it cannot cast a shadow over a curved body or arbitrary receiver because its construction assumes one plane. A fuzzy texture or an ellipse under a character is a deliberate approximation, not a visibility solution. (P3-18)

A shadow volume is the region behind a caster as seen from a light. For a polygonal caster, extrude its silhouette away from the light and close the resulting shape. To test a camera ray, count each entry into the volume as +1 and each exit as −1. If the ray reaches the visible surface with count zero, it is outside all volumes and lit; a positive count means it is inside at least one shadow. The crossing sign can be determined from the ray direction’s dot product with the volume face normal. This supports arbitrary receiving geometry, but every caster polygon may create one or more extra faces. Overlapping volumes lead to many crossings, so the stencil/counting method may be manageable while volume construction, storage and fill work become expensive. (P3-18)

An area light has extent. A point in the umbra is blocked from every part of the source; a point in the penumbra sees some of it. A single point-light projection cannot express that gradual transition. Repeated or layered shadow volumes can approximate partial coverage, but at a high geometry cost. This explains why shadows are a balance between accurate visibility and practical sampling or storage. (P3-18)

Shadow mapping stores the closest depth visible from a light in a depth texture. During the eye-view pass, transform each visible point into the light’s clip space, divide by its homogeneous , map x/y into the light’s texture coordinates and compare its light-space depth with the stored depth at that location. If the point is farther than the stored blocker, it is in shadow. If it is nearer or equal (within a bias), the light is visible. For example, if the map stores depth and the receiver’s projected depth is , the receiver lies behind the surface seen by the light and is shadowed. With depth increasing away from the light, “farther” is a larger value; exact comparisons depend on the depth convention. A small depth bias avoids self-shadowing caused by quantization and interpolation, but too much bias detaches shadows from casters. (P3-18, P3-19)

The lecture’s 2009 derivation walks between eye and light image spaces with inverse view/projection matrices. It emphasizes retaining homogeneous : once a clip point is divided by , that scale is lost and cannot simply be inverted to recover the same homogeneous point. Reconstruct in homogeneous coordinates, transform back through inverse projection and view, then project into the other camera’s space. This makes the coordinate relationship explicit; a typical modern shadow-map shader instead computes light-space coordinates directly from the world-space position before the eye-space projection. (P3-19)

Shadow maps have two coupled resolution limits. A narrow light frustum clips casters or receivers outside its stored view; a very wide frustum spreads a fixed number of texels across more world area, so a single texel covers a larger region and shadows look blocky. Higher resolution helps but costs memory and rendering work. Several lights generally need several maps. Point lights may need multiple views around the source, while a directional light can use an orthographic view; these choices constrain coverage. A point mapped between texel centers also creates aliasing. Percentage-closer filtering (PCF) compares a neighborhood of depth samples and averages the visibility results. A 4×4 filter averages sixteen binary comparisons; if four samples are lit, the fractional result is 4/16. This softens jagged boundaries and can suggest an area light, but ordinary PCF blurs the visibility edge rather than physically integrating all directions from a source. (P3-19)

OpenGL era note. The 2009 lecturer speaks of an OpenGL function for shadow maps and discusses the fixed-function transform pipeline. That is historical context. In modern programmable OpenGL, a common route is to render a depth texture from the light, pass light-space coordinates to a shader, and use a GLSL shadow sampler with depth comparison; the official OpenGL Shading Language 4.60 specification defines these shadow sampler comparisons. Thus the geometric algorithm remains relevant while the API path has changed. (P3-19)

A programmable, differentiable rendering system
Connect to: Monte Carlo rendering; optimization; inverse rendering; physical light transport; CPU/GPU execution.

Mitsuba 2 is a renderer-system paper, not a new surface representation. Its central design problem is how to add different execution modes—scalar, vectorized, GPU, spectral, polarized, and differentiable—without maintaining separate copies of every sampling and shading algorithm. The authors build generic renderer code on Enoki, a C++ array and program-transformation library. A developer writes operations on array-like values; compile-time types choose how those values are represented and which transformations apply. The same high-level algorithm can then be retargeted to scalar values, CPU packets, or GPU arrays.

On the GPU, ordinary eager execution would launch a kernel for each small arithmetic operation. A path tracer performs many simple operations between irregular scene queries, so launch and memory-transfer overhead can dominate. Enoki instead records operations symbolically in a single-static-assignment graph. Reading or otherwise observing the array triggers just-in-time (JIT) compilation of the accumulated graph into a GPU kernel. The first rendering may pay the compilation cost; identical kernels can be cached for later iterations. The approach fuses small operations while allowing a large renderer to build its graph at runtime, without describing the entire codebase in advance.

A renderer’s control flow is irregular. Different rays hit different materials and take different branches. Enoki uses masks to mark which lanes of a vector are active. A vectorized branch computes only for lanes that satisfy its condition. To avoid synchronizing the GPU for every step, code should keep many operations vertical (per-lane) and use horizontal reductions such as all(mask) sparingly. Dynamic method dispatch is more difficult because a vector of rays may point to many material objects. Enoki groups lanes by unique object pointer, calls that material’s method for its active subset, then scatters results back. Gather and scatter also need special derivative rules: in reverse mode, a gather’s gradient becomes a scatter-add, while a scatter’s gradient becomes a gather.

Differentiable rendering creates a second systems problem: reverse-mode automatic differentiation (AD) must retain intermediate values until the output loss is known. A wavefront renderer can store large intersection records and sampled values; at image-scale sample counts, the memory cost can reach multiple gigabytes. Enoki simplifies its computation graph at JIT boundaries. It collapses interior nodes by multiplying derivative weights along paths, trading extra arithmetic for fewer stored nodes. A greedy rule collapses low-cost nodes first. This makes the method a hybrid of forward and reverse differentiation rather than a strict traversal of the original graph. The authors’ Cornell Box measurement shows JIT alone lowers runtime substantially; graph simplification further reduces memory from 2.43 GiB to 1.36 GiB in the reported setting, with a small timing change. This is a benchmark of their 2019 implementation, not a current performance promise.

The system can also change the meaning of its radiance values without duplicating the renderer. For polarization, it represents light with Stokes vectors and material transformations with Mueller matrices. Each Mueller matrix is tied to incident and outgoing reference frames, so those frames must be rotated consistently when light scatters. The renderer uses Mueller-matrix values throughout to keep its interfaces symmetric, even though this performs some unnecessary arithmetic. The paper demonstrates a dielectric between crossed linear polarizers: the glass changes the polarization state so some light passes the second filter. It also enables spectrum-aware transport rather than treating every ray as three fixed RGB numbers; the paper’s renderer samples four wavelengths per ray across 360–830 nm by default.
Differentiable caustics and media

A differentiable renderer can optimize a scene parameter to make a rendered image match a target. For caustics, one example changes a refractive height field so focused light forms a desired image. Another changes a spatially varying refractive index. In a gradient-index medium, rays curve because the index varies with position. The paper writes the ray equation as

The implementation integrates this equation with a Leapfrog step while tracing light. Gradient descent then updates the height field or index grid from the image error. These demonstrations show that a general renderer can support inverse design with a custom differentiable simulation; the authors explicitly say their height-field results do not match purpose-built methods in contrast and precision.
For a scattering medium, the radiative transfer equation (RTE) accounts for light lost to absorption or scattering out of the ray and gained from light scattered into it. In simplified notation,

where is the scattering coefficient, is the phase function, and is transmittance, with extinction . Sampling the distance to the next event normally uses a parameter-dependent probability distribution. Directly differentiating through that sampling transform can fail when it becomes discontinuous—for example, when the sampled event leaves the volume bounds. The paper’s solution is to differentiate the integral before changing variables into primary-sample space, then detach the sampling transform and its probability from the AD graph. This keeps the derivative on the integrand while avoiding an invalid derivative through a discontinuous sampling map.

The authors initially explored delta tracking, which supports unbiased event sampling but can take a variable number of steps and create incoherent GPU execution. They use regular ray marching instead. This gives more coherent GPU work but introduces a small rendering bias. Their smoke-density experiment is synthetic: one view is ambiguous and creates artifacts; matching nine views constrains the density better. Their translucent-slab experiment is also simplified: extinction is homogeneous and monochromatic, while voxel albedo varies. Differentiable rendering improves on a naive color-to-albedo initialization because multiple scattering couples neighboring voxel values.
Coherent bundles for Markov-chain rendering

Mitsuba 2’s vectorization also supports a path-sampling method designed for coherence. A conventional packet tracer may launch many rays together, but their paths quickly diverge into different branches and memory locations. Markov-chain Monte Carlo light transport explores nearby points in primary sample space, the random numbers that define a path. The paper’s coherent pseudo-marginal Metropolis light transport (CPMMLT) smooths the target function by convolving it with a Gaussian in that space:

It estimates this smoothed target with a bundle of nearby paths, evaluating them together in vector lanes. The Gaussian width trades exploration against coherence: nearby samples are more likely to take similar path branches, so the CPU’s vector units and caches do more useful work. The method uses pseudo-marginal MCMC: an unbiased estimate of the smoothed target can be used while preserving the chain’s target distribution. The paper then weights the bundle’s contributions to reconstruct an unbiased estimate of the original, unblurred image. In its tests, CPMMLT evaluates about two to six times more rays per second than the PSSMLT baseline, depending on the scene. Those tests ran on 28-core Intel Xeon Gold 6132 machines; the result is specific to that hardware and comparison.

Practical limits. Reverse-mode AD stores state and may run out of memory as resolution, samples, and path depth grow. Rendering losses have poor local minima, so parameter initialization matters. Ray marching trades a small bias for GPU coherence. The 2019 paper’s software and interfaces are historical: describe the architecture and evidence from the paper, but do not treat its Enoki/Mitsuba 2 API as the current Mitsuba 3 or Dr.Jit API. Its examples demonstrate system flexibility; they do not establish that every inverse-rendering problem is well posed or that one view determines a unique scene.
